chapters.title: Chapter 4: Nudges and Public Policy in India

lessons.title: Swachh Bharat and Social Nudges: Using Norms to Change Public Behavior

children.text: A well-known 2008 hotel experiment tested two versions of the card left in bathrooms asking guests to reuse their towels. One appealed to environmental responsibility: help save the planet. The other simply stated a fact: roughly 75% of guests who stayed in this room reused their towels. The fact outperformed the appeal to conscience by a wide margin. Nobody was told to reuse their towel. Nobody's room key stopped working if they didn't. They were simply told what people like them, in that exact room, actually did, and that alone moved behavior further than an argument about the environment ever managed to.

body.text: Telling people what others like them are already doing can change behavior more reliably than appeals to logic, morality, or self-interest, because humans have a deep, largely automatic tendency to look at what everyone else is doing before deciding what to do themselves. This is the nudge technique behind India's largest public-behavior campaign.

markDefs.definition: A message describing what most people actually do, used to nudge behavior toward the described norm. Distinct from an injunctive norm, which describes what is socially approved or disapproved of.

A message conveying what a community approves or disapproves of, regardless of what people currently do. Complements a descriptive norm, and is especially important when the actual, current behavior is not yet the desired one.

children.text: Psychologists Robert Cialdini, Raymond Reno, and Carl Kallgren drew a sharp distinction in 1990 between two kinds of social norm message. A
describes what most people actually do, like the towel study's 75% figure. An
describes what a community approves or disapproves of, regardless of current behavior. Both work. They work differently, and mixing them up can backfire badly, as the next section shows.

body.title: Size the norm message's effect
body.prompt: In the hotel study, the standard environmental appeal achieved roughly 35% towel reuse. The descriptive social-norm message achieved roughly 44%. By how many percentage points did the norm-based message outperform the standard appeal?
body.explanation: 44% − 35% = 9 percentage points, a relative increase of roughly 9 ÷ 35 ≈ 26% over the standard message. A single factual sentence about what other guests did outperformed a direct appeal to guests' own environmental values.

children.text: Swachh Bharat Mission: India's Largest Social-Norm Campaign

markDefs.definition: The Swachh Bharat Mission, launched 2 October 2014, India's national sanitation campaign focused on eliminating open defecation and building household and community toilets, combining infrastructure subsidies with behavior-change messaging.

children.text: , launched on 2 October 2014, combined two very different tools, and it's worth being precise about which is which. Subsidies for building household toilets, government data has cited more than 10 crore built under the mission, are a genuine economic incentive, not a nudge, the same distinction this chapter has drawn for Aadhaar-linked subsidies and zero MDR. The nudge sits in the behavior-change communication layered on top: campaigns built around visible local progress, celebrity and public-figure endorsements, and community-level sanitation drives using an internationally recognised method called Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS), developed by Kamal Kar and first used in Bangladesh, which brings a village together to directly observe and collectively confront the consequences of open defecation, deliberately triggering shared social discomfort rather than lecturing on hygiene statistics.

The government declared India open defecation free in October 2019, on the mission's fifth anniversary and Mahatma Gandhi's 150th birth anniversary. Independent surveys and researchers have since reported more mixed results in some areas, a reminder that a national declaration and universal, sustained ground-level behavior change are not automatically the same thing, and that toilet construction alone, without continued usage, doesn't finish the job a nudge is meant to do.
Swachh Survekshan: Social Comparison at City Scale

Since 2016, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs has run Swachh Survekshan, an annual cleanliness survey that publicly ranks Indian cities against each other. This applies the same social-comparison psychology behind the towel study at an institutional scale: no city government wants to be seen falling behind comparable peer cities in a published national ranking. It is reputational, not financial, a social-norm nudge aimed at mayors and municipal commissioners rather than individual citizens, showing the same mechanism from this lesson working on an entirely different kind of decision-maker.
The Boomerang Risk: When "Most People Already Do This" Backfires

body.text: A descriptive norm message is only safe to use when the actual current behavior is already the one you want. Telling a community "most households here still don't use a toilet" would state a true baseline while simultaneously signalling that not using one is normal and common, a well-documented boomerang effect. This is exactly why effective sanitation campaigns lead with rising trends, local success stories, and injunctive disapproval of open defecation rather than raw current-usage statistics in places where those statistics are still unfavorable.

body.title: Designing a ward-level campaign
body.scenario: A municipal corporation wants more households in a specific ward to segregate wet and dry waste before collection. A recent internal audit found only 22% of households in the ward currently segregate waste correctly.
body.prompt: Given the boomerang risk covered in this lesson, what should this ward's campaign message say, and what should it avoid saying?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Stating the true current figure directly, "only 22% of households here segregate waste correctly," would be an accurate descriptive norm, but a dangerous one: it also tells the other 78% that not segregating is what most of their neighbours already do, risking a boomerang effect that reinforces the very behavior the campaign wants to change.
2. A safer descriptive framing highlights a positive trend rather than a low baseline, for example "the number of households segregating waste correctly has grown each month this year," if that trend genuinely exists, or focuses on a smaller, comparable reference group already performing well, similar to the hotel study's use of same-room rather than hotel-wide figures.
3. This should be paired with a clear injunctive message, using local leaders, resident welfare associations, or visible signage to establish that correct segregation is the expected, approved standard for the ward, independent of the current adoption rate.
4. The campaign should also track segregation rates over time and be willing to switch the descriptive message to the real figure once it crosses a point where citing it would reinforce compliance rather than undermine it.

body.title: Social norm, or a different mechanism?
body.question: A city's waste-collection app defaults every new user's household to a "segregated waste" collection slot, requiring a manual setting change to switch to unsegregated collection. Which mechanism is primarily at work here, distinct from the social-norm techniques covered in this lesson?
options: An injunctive norm, because segregation is socially approved of
The default effect, because segregated collection is what happens unless the user actively changes it
A descriptive norm, because it states what most households already do
The boomerang effect, because it risks normalising unsegregated collection
body.explanation: Pre-setting an option that applies unless someone actively changes it is the default effect from Chapter 2, not a social norm message. This lesson's descriptive and injunctive norms work by communicating information about others' behavior or approval, not by pre-selecting an outcome.

body.title: Name the norm type
body.textWithBlank: A message stating what a community approves or disapproves of, independent of what people currently do, is called an ___ norm.
body.explanation: Injunctive norms are especially important when the current, real behavior isn't yet the desired one, since a plainly stated descriptive norm in that situation risks normalising the very behavior a campaign is trying to change.

body.title: Where did Community-Led Total Sanitation come from?

children.text: CLTS was developed by Kamal Kar around 2000 while evaluating a sanitation programme in Bangladesh, where he found that subsidised toilet construction alone hadn't changed open defecation habits nearly as much as expected. His alternative approach deliberately avoided subsidies and hygiene lectures, instead facilitating a community "walk of shame" through their own open defecation sites, letting the community itself calculate how much faecal matter they were collectively producing and ingesting through contaminated water and food. The resulting disgust and social pressure, generated by the community for itself rather than imposed from outside, proved far more durable than externally imposed rules, and the method has since been adopted across South Asia and Africa, including within parts of India's Swachh Bharat implementation.

body.label: Swachh Bharat Mission's launch
body.context: India was declared open defecation free five years later, in October 2019, though independent surveys have reported more mixed results in some areas since.

cards.definition: A message describing what most people actually do, used to nudge behavior toward the described norm.
A message describing what a community approves or disapproves of, independent of current behavior.
The risk that stating a true but unfavorable descriptive norm normalises the very behavior a campaign is trying to reduce.

A sanitation behavior-change method, developed by Kamal Kar, that facilitates communities confronting the consequences of open defecation themselves, generating internal social pressure rather than relying on external rules.
India's annual cleanliness survey ranking cities against each other, applying social-comparison pressure at the institutional level since 2016.

points: Descriptive norm messages, stating what most people already do, can outperform appeals to logic or morality, as the hotel towel study's roughly 9 percentage point gain demonstrated.

Injunctive norms, stating what a community approves or disapproves of, matter most precisely when current behavior isn't yet the desired one, which is when a plain descriptive statistic risks backfiring.

Swachh Bharat Mission combined a genuine economic incentive, toilet-construction subsidies, with social-norm nudges like CLTS's community-triggered social pressure, and the two are worth telling apart rather than crediting one mechanism for the other's results.
Swachh Survekshan shows social-comparison nudges scaling beyond individuals to institutions, using published city rankings to create reputational pressure on municipal decision-makers.

A national policy declaration and sustained ground-level behavior change are not automatically the same thing, which is why well-designed campaigns keep measuring real behavior rather than resting on the initial announcement.
